title: Terminating and Repeating Decimals
short: Divide to change a fraction to a decimal that ends or repeats.
trouble: Students stop dividing too early and write 2/3 as 0.6.

blocks.html: A fraction is a division: $\frac{3}{8}$ means $3 \div 8$. With long division you can turn any fraction into a decimal. Sometimes the division stops; sometimes it goes on forever, in a pattern.

Divide the numerator by the denominator. The decimal either terminates (the remainder reaches 0) or repeats (a block of digits repeats forever). A bar marks the repeating block: $\frac{2}{3} = 0.\overline{6}$ and $\frac{1}{6} = 0.1\overline{6}$.

When you divide by 6, every remainder is one of $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$. If a remainder is 0, the division ends. If not, a remainder must come back within a few steps, and from then on the division does exactly the same thing again, so the digits repeat. A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator has no prime factors except 2 and 5, the factors of 10.

blocks.name: g7-longdiv
blocks.cap: Press "Next digit" and watch the remainders. When one comes back, the digits repeat. Try other fractions too.

blocks.title: A terminating decimal
steps: The remainder is 0, so it stops: $0.375$.

blocks.title: A repeating decimal
steps: The remainder 2 keeps coming back, so the 6 repeats forever: $0.666\ldots = 0.\overline{6}$.

blocks.title: The bar on part of it
steps: Remainder 5 is where we started (5 ÷ 11), so "45" repeats: $0.4545\ldots = 0.\overline{45}$.

blocks.html: Stopping too early and writing $\frac{2}{3} = 0.6$. That is only $\frac{6}{10} = \frac{3}{5}$. Even $0.67$ is a rounded value, not equal to $\frac{2}{3}$. Keep dividing until the remainder is 0 or a remainder repeats.
